newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Annan renews call for troops in eastern Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Annan renews call for troops in eastern Zaire.

text.p: U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan on Thursday renewed calls for troops in eastern Zaire to protect aid to Rwandan refugees fleeing from fighting in the region.
Annan, his spokesman said, preferred a political solution to the conflict that included a ceasefire and talks among all parties that Zaire has accepted.
"But if that is not possible he feels we must consider how to provide this protection to aid workers and refugees without a ceasefire," spokesman Fred Eckhard said.

He said Annan agreed with a foreign minister who told him that it was "strange that the media could visit eastern Zaire, Mrs Sadako Ogata could visit eastern Zaire, aid workers could visit eastern Zaire but it is too dangerous for troops to go there." Ogata is the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees.

Annan met Mohammed Sahnoun, his special representative for Central Africa, who arrived in New York late on Wednesday and was consulting with Security Council members on the fighting between rebels and Zairean government forces.
But so far France appears to be the only major nation supporting a multinational force, which was organised by Canada late last year but then called off when many refugees began returning home.

The United States said on Wednesday it was not ready to make a commitment to a multinational force at this time. "We don't think the time is right to make that decision," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.

But the concept of a force also differs among various parties from what Annan apparently had in mind to protect refugees and relief workers, many of whom have now been expelled from the conflict areas by Zairean authorities.

Zaire, which appears to be losing militarily in the east, wants "international monitors" to oversee a withdrawal of foreign troops and implementation of a U.N. peace plan that calls for a ceasefire and political negotiations.
But the rebels say that Zaire's concept would serve to prop up the government of ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko, the country's strongman who is recuperating in Europe.

Zaire, which has hired mercenaries, accuses neighbouring Uganda, Rwanda and Burundi of sending in troops to fight alongside rebels of the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL) closing in on the northeastern capital of Kisangani. All three countries deny the accusations.
While more than a million Rwandan refugees have returned, up to 500,000 others are still in Zaire, many unaccounted for and others believed dead.

Among the refugees are members of the Hutu militia and former Rwandan government army responsible for the 1994 Rwanda genocide of more than 500,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus. Fearing revenge, the Hutus fled Rwanda to eastern Zaire after the Tutsis fought their way into power in 1994.

Last October the rebel onslaught, led by ethnic Tutsis living in Zaire, broke up most of the refugee camps, with the Hutu fighters joining the Zairean government. The rebels took up arms when authorities tried to expel them.
